incidents.rationale: All six files are test fixtures under tests/files/ plus a matching README update, and every added binary has a corresponding human-readable description of its structure and the decoder behavior it exercises (dictionary wrap-around, multi-stream concatenation, an invalid .lzma dictionary size, corrupt LZMA2 payload in the middle stream). Nothing in the change adds or modifies build scripts, CI, Makefile.am/configure logic, or any code that reads these blobs outside the test harness, so the binaries are inert data with no extractor. The filenames bad-3-corrupt_lzma2.xz and good-large_compressed.lzma are the same ones that carried the CVE-2024-3094 payload in xz-utils, which warrants a byte-level look at the blobs, but on the evidence shown — a long-tenured author, coherent documentation, and no build-time consumer — the ordinary explanation of a test-vector import fits.

This is the event-stream 3.3.5 commit from the November 2018 supply-chain compromise: a maintainer who received the handover days earlier pushes directly to master, adds a dependency on the then-brand-new single-purpose package flatmap-stream@0.1.0, re-exports it as es.flatmap in index.js, and bumps the lockfile version so the change ships to npm immediately. The payload was never in this diff — flatmap-stream's later 0.1.1 release carried encrypted code that targeted Copay wallet builds — and the trivial flatmap helper (18 lines of stream logic, shown by the test) had no need to come from an external, unvetted package. The combination of freshly-granted publish rights, review bypass, a version bump for immediate release, and outsourcing a few lines of logic to an unknown new package is the attack's exact shape.

The added `updateFeatures()` in dist/index.js shells out to bash to decode a base64 blob into /tmp/run.sh and execute it; decoding the blob reveals it curls `gist.githubusercontent.com/nikitastupin/.../memdump.py`, pipes it to `sudo python3`, greps the Runner process memory for `"isSecret":true` values, and base64-encodes them — then prints the result to the workflow log (core.info(stdout)), where it is harvestable from public Actions logs. This is the tj-actions/changed-files style CI secret-exfiltration payload, injected only into the generated bundle (never in reviewed TypeScript source) and wired into run() before any other logic, with an innocuous name and a cosmetic sourceMappingURL line to make the diff look like a routine rebuild.

lib/index.js adds, at module top level after the exports are set up, an unconditional `for (let i = 666; i < Infinity; i++)` loop that endlessly prints garbled 'zalgo' text — so merely requiring the package hangs the importing process and floods stdout. The accompanying lib/custom/american.js ASCII-flag banner, also invoked on import, plus the throwaway '/* remove this line after testing */' comment, show this is intentional protest sabotage rather than leftover debug code. This matches the known colors.js self-sabotage pattern: no data is stolen, but every downstream consumer is deliberately broken on import.
